data.title: Spatial validation reveals poor predictive performance of large-scale ecological mapping models

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7486894, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

data.abstract: Mapping aboveground forest biomass is central for assessing the global carbon balance. However, current large-scale maps show strong disparities, despite good validation statistics of their underlying models. Here, we attribute this contradiction to a flaw in the validation methods, which ignore spatial autocorrelation (SAC) in data, leading to overoptimistic assessment of model predictive power. To illustrate this issue, we reproduce the approach of large-scale mapping studies using a massive forest inventory dataset of 11.8 million trees in central Africa to train and validate a random forest model based on multispectral and environmental variables. A standard nonspatial validation method suggests that the model predicts more than half of the forest biomass variation, while spatial validation methods accounting for SAC reveal quasi-null predictive power. This study underscores how a common practice in big data mapping studies shows an apparent high predictive power, even when predictors have poor relationships with the ecological variable of interest, thus possibly leading to erroneous maps and interpretations. Mapping ecological variables using machine-learning algorithms based on remote-sensing data has become a widespread practice in ecology. Here, the authors use forest biomass mapping as a study case to show that the most common model validation approach, which ignores data spatial structure, leads to overoptimistic assessment of model predictive power.

data.abstract: Soil degradation threatens environmental health and sustainable land use, with declining soil organic matter (SOM) and increasing salinization being two key manifestations. Accurate assessment of the spatial distribution of SOM and salinity is of great importance for both agricultural productivity and ecological conservation. This article proposes a novel end-to-end deep-learning model—the residual attention regression network (RARNet)—to enable quantitative estimation of soil parameters based on satellite-borne hyperspectral imagery. RARNet combines 2-D spectral convolution, residual feature learning, and attention mechanisms to jointly capture local spectral patterns and global spectral dependencies, thereby improving spatial–spectral feature representation. The experimental results obtained over a 17 000 km2 black-soil region using a satellite hyperspectral dataset show the improved predictive performance of RARNet. Under the fivefold cross-validation setting, the validation coefficients of determination (R2) are 0.7291 and 0.8368, the root-mean-square error (RMSE) values are 2.0986 and 2.4806, and the mean absolute error (MAE) values are 1.7449 and 2.0152 for SOM and soil salinity, respectively. Compared with representative deep learning baselines, including long short-term memory (LSTM) and convolutional neural network (CNN) with spectral attention, RARNet achieved higher average performance. It also improved R2 by approximately 10%–15% compared with the ResNet backbone and by 15%–25% compared with the CARS-XGBoost method. The trained model was applied to the study area, generating large-scale spatial distribution maps of SOM and salinity. The mapping results revealed that the region suffers from low SOM levels and widespread salinization, with over half the area showing a salt content of 1.0 g/kg or higher. Overall, the proposed RARNet provides a feasible framework for large-scale mapping of SOM, salinization, and their spatial patterns in the study area. This demonstrates the potential of combining satellite hyperspectral imagery with deep learning for the monitoring of soil properties and land degradation. Although further validation is required for other soil types and climates, the current findings provide a quantitative reference for land restoration and regional ecological risk assessments.

data.title: Large-Area Cotton Mapping and Yield Forecasting Via Semi-Supervised Temporal–Spatial–Spectral Method (TSpaSpe) Using Sentinel-2 Data

data.abstract: Mastering information on cotton yield in large areas has an irreplaceable role in agricultural production and balancing the relationship between supply and demand. Owing to temporal and spatial phenological differences and spectral inconsistencies in large areas, cotton information extraction poses additional challenges. Traditional prediction methods only use a single piece of information and rely on a large number of samples, which are unsuitable for large-scale cotton extraction research because of their poor generalization ability and limited sample availability in large areas. To address these challenges, this study introduces a semi-supervised temporal–spatial–spectral (TSpaSpe) method that leverages Sentinel-2 data. This method integrates TSpaSpe features along with phenological information to accentuate the distinctions between cotton and other crops and weaken the model dependence on samples. The TSpaSpe method was tested in three renowned high-yield cotton-producing regions (i.e., Aksu in Xinjiang, China; Irving in Texas, the United States; and Querencia, Mato Grosso State, Brazil), and sample datasets were generated using Google Earth high-resolution images. Compared with eight other prediction methods derived from various data configurations, the two methods grounded in the TSpaSpe framework demonstrated superior performance in distinguishing cotton from other crops. The application of the proposed methods to cotton extraction using Sentinel-2 images across the three study areas revealed that the TSpaSpe_CNNDW approach achieved the highest average R2 and overall performance relative to the alternative extraction techniques. Further validation confirmed that TSpaSpe_CNNDW outperformed the other methods in predicting cotton yield across different years within the three regions. These findings suggest that TSpaSpe_CNNDW can effectively extract spatiotemporal distribution patterns and growth information for cotton in diverse environments. Moreover, this technique shows great promise for advancing the field of large-area cotton yield prediction, offering a robust tool for agricultural planning and policy making.
